Tell me if you know this game: it's a first-person puzzle game set in a long abandoned outpost. You lug around a special gun that has two different (but related) firing modes, and are tasked with solving various physics-based puzzles, some of which require you to manipulate a certain geometrically-shaped object. It's Portal, right? It's not, of course: I'm talking about 'The Ball'. The Ball *so* wants to be the next Portal game -it has all the trappings- and completely fails to achieve that goal. While Portal has a sublime mix of intriguing puzzles and an interesting setting, The Ball's puzzles are rarely a challenge and the setting is uninspired. Quite simply, The Ball is *dull*.  The game started out as a total-conversion for Unreal and, had it remained only that, I would have been more forgiving. After all, free software from an independent up-and-coming group of developers is worth the benefit of the doubt. But when packaged and sold at retail, I expect a bit more. While the controls are adequate, the puzzles are a repetitive 'push the eponymous ball onto button' (often mixed with some atrocious jumping challenges) that very quickly wear out their welcome. The game environments are bland and filled with pointless dead areas where nothing happens.  Other reviews indicate that the game does pick up right near the end, but I never got that far; the tedium of the first three quarters of the game wore me out. Rumors of a few interesting puzzles a dozen levels down the line just isn't enough to keep me trudging through the characterless boredom that comprises the rest of the game.

The Ball is a fairly interesting action puzzler. The main draw is the fantastical art direction, which is heavily inspired by the Aztecs, Incans, Mayans, and even the Egyptians to some extent. All of these wonderful cultures have been woven together into the Aztec legends of Quetzacoatl, with the art and architecture being blended with lo-fi tech from the alien race.  The gameplay is fairly simple: Guide ball from room to room, use it to complete puzzles and defend yourself. Every so often, the game introduces a new mechanic (either in the world, or the Ball itself) that modifies the gameplay drastically. These moments are excellent, though they are few & far between. The Ball could have been much better served if more inventive ways to manipulate it and the world were explored throughout the campaign.  The story (as presented without finding the secrets) is vague and not terribly interesting. We never learn much about the alien race aside from what you can assume from the world they inhabit below ground. The king (antagonist? protagonist?) is simililarly left unexplored and does not interact with the player at all.  All in all, a fairly fun game which just falls short of the promise of the world Teotl Studios have created.   Beautiful art, great music, and expansive levels make this a worthwhile purchase when on sale.

Critics loved it and the game went on to win numerous awards from both ModDB and the Make Something Unreal contests. While it stands as proof to how ambitious mods can be, it's now also an example of how some freebies should stay free.  The Ball, while categorized under the puzzle genre, barely felt like one. Very minimal thinking is required for the first 2/3 of the game. At best, The Ball is a beautiful, but extremely mediocre and repetitive bore-fest.  It's only until the final 1/3 of the game that the developers decide to mix things up with new enemies and unique ball modifications. But by then, a chunk of their audience will have already lost interest.  There is just a certain quality consumers expect from retail games. As a free mod, The Ball might exceed every gamer's expectation. But, as a retail product, it lacks the ingredients to make it challenging, exciting, and fun.  Grade: C

I remember when I first saw The Ball pop up on Steam and I got quite intrigued. I had pipe dreams in my head about using the ball so solve almost acrobatic puzzles using football style trick shots or impressively complicated rube-goldberg devices. I didn't buy it in in the end though. However it popped up again as part of a Tripwire Interactive bundle so I finally grabbed it.   Straight off the bat I can say that The Ball isn't terrible, it's not Duke Nukem awful or Call of Duty boring. But it's not impressive either. It's a sort of safe affair through out.  No where did I find the satisfying trick shot or juggling that I dreamed up. But that's not to say the puzzles are boring. They're fairly straight forward and no one should really find themselves stuck at any point. Some of them are still pretty clever in themselves. But the main pitfalls of the puzzles (and these are major problems with the game) is that The Ball, the main focus of the game that you drag about, never really does anything but act as another way to press buttons you cannot reach. Well, that's not strictly true but more on that later. The puzzles do not really expand to include new concepts or mutations ( again there is an exception but later on) passed ' this button needs pressing, get to it'.   There is also a strange problem with the pacing of the over all game. The core mistake is that the game gives you little to no motivation to carry on. There is quite little reward. There's no narrative to get into, no rewards or things given to the player. You just seem to 'do' and then move on to 'do' again. The game attempts to break itself up with some random and ultimately pointless vehicle sections (mostly on a rail and with one controllable vehicle) that just seem to stretch out phases of nothingness.   The problem of lacking purpose persists into Boss fights also. For example (Oh and spoiler alert. Oh wait ! No narrative! Nevermind!) at some point you and your ball get trapped in a small square arena with a cannon that shoots bombs that you activate with a button, and a 15ft enraged zombie gorilla (yep). The solution is, obviously, to blast furry undead ♥♥♥♥ with the cannon. This is pleasantly easier said than done. Until you die. At which then the game spits you out back into the arena as if nothing happened and all challenge just dissipates. What was a hectic boss fight becomes just another puzzle but with a random, annoying element (that happens to be a 15ft zombie monkey). This nonexistent difficulty curve is through the entire game mind you, so it's pointless to add enemies in it at all.   But some positive points: The game really innovates for about 5 seconds near the end. With one very small puzzle which adds new elements to the game. The Ball suddenly has this fun low-gravity field sorrounding it and much of the puzzles have you throwing the ball, jumping into the field as it cruises through the air and leaping out of it onto a far distant platform and turning in time to catch the ball again. All in one smooth move. And that is cool. Then the game snatches that fun from you and says 'right, that's enough satisfaction for you, into the pointless ♥♥♥♥ing vehicle you go'.   If the Ball dared to change things up a bit, added a bit more personality and varied the aesthetic it would of been a killer fun game. But as it stands it's merely safe and easy.  Worth a quid or two if it's on sale. Don't pay full price unless you're a serious lover of balls.   (Look mum! My degree from a dissolved university was well worth the 3 years of infinate stress and life long debt!)

The ball itself is a simple artifact with only two controls, hammer, and recall, allowing you to bowl the ball down hallways, or draw it back to you as needed. The Ball with some pretty big flaws.  First, I'll start with the good: The environment design. The vast caves and ancient mayan/aztec/central american cities are very captivating to look at and explore. There are some great vistas in the game. Similarly, the design of the enemies is pretty good. Also, the ball puzzles are, for the most part, fun, if quite easy to solve.  However, there are a lot of problems. The first thing that hits you is the wya the game is renderd. It has a sort of 'cell-shaded-but-not-really' feel to it, and it looks as if someone was toying with the saturation filter a little too much at times. But this isn't anything major, and is probably more a matter of personal taste.  One of the biggest gripes I have with this game is the level design. Yes, I just praised the environments, you would think the level design was good too, no? Unfortunately, this game suffers very badly from 'invisible wall syndrome'. Rather than design the areas you can walk around to not have areas you can cheat your way around, the devs simply slapped an invisible wall wherever you're not supposed to go. This is really jarring and annoying when I encounter it in a game, especially one that involves having to more around an object like the ball. It ggets so bad that at one point, thanks to a physics glitch, I had trapped myself floating in mid air, standing on top of an invisible wall, and was unable to get back into the level because it was there.  Also, on the subject on exploring the nvironment. There comes times when you try to explore the area to find more 'secrets', but find yourself being forced onto the next area because you solved a puzzle or boss fight too quickly, which prevents you from finding the secrets. This is very annoying.  There are also some 'boss' fights which range from incredibly easy to beat to downright impossible without dying many times first. You shouldn't have to rely on the game saving your progress on dying to get past bosses.  I would also like to touch on the story. It starts with you trapped down a hole. Fair enough, an archaeologist is bound to have that happen to them once or twice. But then it appears they have no rope to send down the hole. And apparently they need a crane to lift you out. None of this makes sense, the hole isn't really that deep, and pretty early on in the game, the player mysteriously produces some rope with which to tie the ball to things.  So in short, The Ball is a fairly mediocre puzzle game, which if you're just a new and casual player, you may enjoy, but if you've played games for a while, you will very easily spot the flaws in it.

I have owned this game for years, and played it  a lot . I'd say a good third of that gameplay is from my currently-in-progress guide. If you've come here from The Solus Project, you should note that TSP is The Ball's spiritual successor. It is not a direct sequel. While you can safely play TSP without ever having played The Ball, I highly recommend playing The Ball first. Having now played both, I can see very direct connections that both make more sense, and are more exciting to find, if you are already familiar with certain things from The Ball.  The Ball gets compared to Portal for obvious reasons: It's a puzzle game with simple tools that began as a mod and became a standalone by popular demand. This is fairly light, as far as puzzle games go. You aren't going to spend hours screaming in frustration, but that doesn't mean the solution to everything will be immeidately apparent.  The Ball experiments with a few different mechanics, but doesn't dwell on any of them for too long. Nothing hangs around for long enough to get old - unless you have a distaste for Aztec aesthetics, in which case you may want to check out the screenshots above. Some sections of this game are relaxed and can be taken at your own pace. Others require a modicum of haste.  I can't quite define why I'm so enamoured with The Ball. It has a simple charm. It does what it needs to do (puzzles, adventure) and doesn't add anything unnecessary on top - but there are extra things to explore (secrets and bonus levels) should you choose to. The story isn't particularly complex, and you do have to go out of your way to learn all of it, but the basics are literally impossible to miss.  If you enjoyed Portal for the exploration and puzzles, you'll probably enjoy The Ball. If you're seeking The Solus Project 0.1, you might be disappointed, but I would still recommend picking this up on sale.

A trail of different coloured balls are pushed along a track by a beetle, and using a launcher, you must fire a randomly coloured ball into the trail, being careful to place it next to a ball of the same colour. When at least three collide with one another they'll be eliminated. Eliminate all balls (which destroys the beetle) before the trail reaches the end of the track to pass to the next stage.  Everything starts off sedately enough as the convoy makes its way slowly along some fairly straightforward tracks. But as the stages progress, the whole thing moves faster and tracks become ever more elaborate, criss-crossing over itself or being intertwined with a second track with another trail being simultaneously pushed along it, as well as additional colours being added to complicate the assortment and make matches more difficult to obtain.  Thankfully, there are power-ups to aid you as reward for clearing balls, such as wild balls which will match with any colour, fireballs which destroy all balls within a certain radius, lightning strikes that fire a vertical bolt up the screen to clear everything in its path, and upgrades that temporarily slow or even completely halt movement of the trail briefly.  It's a casual time-waster that's fun to dip in and out of every so often, but while early stages are fun enough and easy-going enough to allow you to take your time setting up massive combos and chain reactions, by the back third or quarter of the main adventure mode, I found the pace and number of colours to manage to be too frantic to be all that much fun anymore. Rather than setting up an epic set piece of destruction, it feels more like damage control as you focus on the immediate threat at the front of the trail and are constantly trying to put that fire out. The front end of play is slow and considered and the back end of it is reflexive, and that's actually where I started to get bored as I slipped into autopilot for one stage after another.  Everything has an Egyptian theme to it in both look and sound, along with an overworld map screen that I don't understand the purpose of given that stages themselves repeat and have no shared theme to link them together into a combined 'world' on a map that has what seems to be a completely arbitrary stage number attached to it. But there are plenty of stages along the way and many hours to sink into this across three difficulties.  I got the game in a bundle for a few euro and could live with the purchase more easily that way, as I wouldn't be in a hurry to pay the full asking price for it. But I guess what it's worth is up to each person individually, so if this sounds like your kind of thing that you're willing to drop the full amount on, then go for it.

In grand Popcap tradition, Zuma's Revenge is a simple game to learn, but exciting and satisfying to play and play and play. The premise has a line of multi-colored marbles inching their way along a pre-defined path towards an ultimate drop-dead point and you have to shoot similar colored marbles at the line in order to create matches of at least three marbles. Different bonuses will allow greater control over the advancing line, but the real progress comes from simply being dextrous enough to notice the matches and quickly fire accurately. The game is relatively stress free until the final levels when the game starts throwing interlocking looped paths which block your ability to manipulate the entire line and forcing you to act quick and precise to keep things managable. At certain points the game changes and you face off against different 'boss' characters which employ subtle variations to the game techniques. The experience prooves to be very satisfying and quite rewarding.

Zuma's Revenge is another well made casual action puzzle game by PopCap Games. The game is brightly colored, easy to learn, but occasionally quite challenging. The sound design and tropical theme work very well together and none of the effects used become to grating or repetitious. Altogether I would recommend this game to any of my friends who like casual puzzle games, as this title has both the gameplay and polish necessary to deliver hours of entertainment.

In grand Popcap tradition, Zuma's Revenge is a simple game to learn, but exciting and satisfying to play and play and play. The premise has a line of multi-colored marbles inching their way along a pre-defined path towards an ultimate drop-dead point and you have to shoot similar colored marbles at the line in order to create matches of at least three marbles. Different bonuses will allow greater control over the advancing line, but the real progress comes from simply being dextrous enough to notice the matches and quickly fire accurately. The game is relatively stress free until the final levels when the game starts throwing interlocking looped paths which block your ability to manipulate the entire line and forcing you to act quick and precise to keep things managable. At certain points the game changes and you face off against different 'boss' characters which employ subtle variations to the game techniques. The experience prooves to be very satisfying and quite rewarding.

Pop Cap games are truly a mixed bag. On one hand, you could get lucky with Plants Vs. Zombies or Peggle. But, on the other, you could be playing Zuma's Revenge. Before continuing, I would like to note that this review is coming from solely playing the adventure mode. Zuma's Revenge's adventure mode has you playing as a frog on an island, making your way through on your adventure.   The gameplay seems to be simple, Zuma having a color ball and having to match three or more of the same color of ball on the track before the balls reach a certain point to which you have to restart the round. On paper, this seems quite simple but the game needs polish as it becomes frustrating when the game solely relies on luck to win the round. The music to the game is simple but, unfortunately, lacking. The same song always plays, allowing for no diversity and not giving the player any reason to keep listening.  In adventure mode, the frog most fight bosses but it doesn't feel like there are any at all. For the most part, the bosses are simple, the only boss which is noticable is the last one because of it's three-stage gauntlet.   To wrap up, Zuma's Revenge seems to be attempting to ride on the success of Peggle, a game which came out two years prior. However, where Peggle is both skill intensive and luck intensive, Zuma's Revenge simply relies on luck to get through. I did put in almost eight hours playing this game but that wasn't because I was having fun, that's because luck wasn't on my side. When the right set-up and power-ups came up, I was able to finally get past a stage that troubled me, no skill involved. If you have the money and would like to play a mindless game, buy Peggle instead.

Breakout Invaders is a mash up of both Space Invaders and Breakout. If you are not familiar with those titles one is a vertical shoot em up and the other is pretty much reverse Pong in where you try to break all the blocks and not let the ball pass your goal. There are 100 levels and each level usually changes how the game plays. One mission you will be tasked with breaking all the blocks and in the next you may be tasked with defending blocks from aliens using your ball and lasers as a weapon. Lasers are used by either right clicking or using the alt key and can be used to destroy blocks or damage enemies though whether you have unlimited ammo depends level from level. You also have a missile which causes far more damage and has splash damage but you can only carry up to 10. In later levels they introduce metal gates that won't allow you to shoot blocks and must use a ball to reach them.  That is easier said than done. The physics in Breakout Invaders are completely insane and have no logic behind them at times. Your ball is the bounciest thing in the universe and hitting it with the edge of your paddle does not bounce it to the side like you would expect. It's a hard thing to explain but imagine playing Pong and the ball always going straight up instead of being able to bounce it off the sides of the screen when you learn to hit it properly. Unlike Breakout or Space Invaders this has a pinball like perspective to the maps instead of a simple 2D plane, so that adds some more complexity to it. Destroying castles and cites is great fun even though most of the times you will break blocks by chance instead of skill. Unfortunately later on they introduce small pipes that you must shoot your ball into to reach an area but the controls and physics are just not up to par to require the precision they so those end up being a pain.  You can control the game with either your mouse or your arrow keys but the mouse is way too sensitive for my liking. It works perfectly fine with the arrows keys but in some levels you are required to use the mouse which is pretty annoying. Which brings me to my biggest gripe with the game. Every level seems to have some kind of cheap gimmick like having 10 balls on screen for 2 minutes or having to destroy some blocks but having one paddle and goal on each side of the screen, making it feel like a game of Warlords that makes you have to control all players at once . The game is at it's best when it has you just breaking blocks yet every level has some kind of nuisance to break the flow once you start to actually have fun. It really makes it feel like a collection of mini games instead of modes built around the basic mechanics of Breakout and would have benefited from having them as extra features instead of being forced into the base game.  Another good portion of the game will have you fighting the aliens from Space Invaders and these are in my opinion the worst part of the game. Your paddle is way too large and makes avoiding projectiles a real pain plus you still have to worry about your ball. It's like being the fat guy in a game of paintball and having to text your boss in the middle of a gunfight. You do usually have infinite ammo for your laser but when you are down to the last few aliens they become extremely bullet spongy. It is insane how many hits they take and I actually thought my game was glitched until one of the three finally exploded. That is due to the tacked on upgrade system this game has. You will need to collect money to buy new ships or to upgrade your firepower. The problem is the game is incredibly stingy with money and the only way to get more is completing a level so you have two options, either grind some prior levels or deal with it. With that and having a gimmick every level it is like the devs think we have the attention span of a newt and need some kind of motive to play the game instead of it simply playing for the fun of it like say the two games they so proudly mention.   Both Space Invaders and Breakout were about skill. They were both based around improving the player, not the ship with extra firepower or the paddle with more speed. They gave you all the tools you needed from the get go and designed the game around that. Breakout Invader on the other hand simply beefs up the enemies and hopes you spent your limited cash correctly if you don't want to spend the next couple of minutes slowly chipping off the enemies health. It honestly would have been a better game if you had a single ship, no upgrades and optional game modes like the games it was inspired by. Moving on from that rant, there are other power-ups besides rockets and lasers. There are meteors that will destroy parts of the map, items that either shrink or increase your paddle and one that makes balls move faster. One small gripe is that items come down too slowly and would benefit from a bit more speed going down. Can be a bit bothersome waiting for it to makes its way down the screen while keeping track of the ball.  Environments are not pretty bland and takes quite some time to see any new ones. Music is a mixed bag, it ranges from good to terrible. Some sound effects sound right out of the late 70's which is nice. It was a fun game when it played like Breakout but with power ups, though every other gimmick was sub-par. If you are a fan of Space Invaders I wouldn't bother with this game. If you are a fan of Breakout there is a bit of fun to be had here but the good will ultimately be outweighed due to having to put up with gimmick after gimmick just to get to the next level that plays like Breakout. It is such an annoying design decision, it is like playing one level of one game, switching to a few other games and then going back to the one you actually like. Having them as different game modes instead of lumping them together to have “100 levels” would have been preferred. It's a shame, it could have been a decent little throwback but the devs spread themselves too thin and choose quantity over the quality of the gameplay.

Marble Mayhem Fragile Ball is a simple and intriguing 2d puzzle board game that reminds me of the original toys I used to play as a kid.  Here is a link for anyone who is curious to what I'm talking about:   Marble Board Game   [i.imgur.com]   Pro-tip: if you have a  mouse with DPI settings   [en.wikipedia.org]  then you will be able to fine tune the rate at which you tilt the game board, however depending on the level there is a hard limit to how much you can tilt the board one way or the other.  The controls are fairly basic and simple:  Moving your mouse left/right will tilt the game board level left or right and make the marble roll a certain direction.  Clicking LMB will cause your marble to respawn.  Scroll wheel will zoom in/out.  Also another thing that took me a while to learn was how there are different types of marbles such as glass and rubber ones. If your marble falls more than a certain distance it may shatter when it lands (I believe this also depends on the type of marble and object it lands on such as brick/wood).  At the moment I'm currently “stuck” on level 16 although from my experience so far I rate it a ★★★★ out of ★★★★★ for what it sets out to do, which is to be a simple – easy to pick up and learn marble game.

Marble Mayhem Fragile Ball on PC 7.5/10 Review after 5 hrs and 37 / 100 mazes completed.  A little ball rolling around in 2D maze trying to get out by the door in the corner. And yet Marble Mayhem is so much more: Wild mazes with moving plates, gaps, skateboard ramps, spikes, water, and did I mention extreme angles? Sometimes this feels more like soccer. If the ball gets hit too hard - it shatters - start again…. Addictive.  Mechanics: Moving your mouse rotates the maze and gravity moves the ball; the controls are tight and the physics are spot on. Mouse rotational sensitivity is adjustable. Patience with trial and error always pay off in games requiring the mastery of physics…. I did not rage quit a single time !  Graphics are basic and audio is simple; both need polish.  Full price on Steam seems rather extreme, but if you find it on sale you may be pleasantly surprised by this digital version of a childhood classic XD  Oct 2015

Despite the thumbs-down, this is definitely a game a minority of people will enjoy (and I'm still trying to finish some of the final stages), but let me explain.  If this title were cut down into about half, maybe two-thirds of the 100* stages, and they cherry-picked only the best, you would have an incredibly solid little puzzle game. The issue comes in that there are sets of levels I would refer to as 'poorly designed'.They're trial and error machines with no hints or ability to solve them short of flinging yourself to death on the course repeatedly. Examples would be multiple which start you at a high point, then give you a left or right direction to fall in. For one thing, the game's title is spot-on: your ball is fragile and tapping ANYTHING over a certain velocity will kill you**, so if you pick the wrong path: bam, dead. Alright, but then what happens when a level is nothing but left/right paths where you have to memorize which is correct and which isn't? Or a single left/right fall but one side has a cushion at the bottom to catch you (which you need to aim for precisely, those ain't big) and the other doesn't. And you have to blind-aim your momentum to land on something that's way off screen.  I hope you're beginning to get my point here.  But at the other end of the scale, there are stages which create some really fun challenges, where you have a full 360-degree playfield and you're working your momentum in platforming you don't see in anything else, managing momentum and angle of rotation and trying to find the exit before you can even maneuver down to it. When the game gives you the freedom in a stage to approach it however you like, it really takes off for a few minutes at a time.  Also, I feel this needs to be stated: this game is ugly as sin, consisting of nothing but stock textures used over and over in eye-searing ways. I think there are under 10 textures in the entire game, and sometimes they will be backgrounds, sometimes foregrounds, and usually in clashing, jarring fashion.  * I presume there are 100 levels. Where I'm currently at, around 15 tiles on a 100-tile board refuse to open up, whether I clear things adjacent to them or not. ** Except in 'Super Ball' stages. These are poorly designed for other reasons, because you're invincible to physics damage in them, but basically controlling rubber and a lot of them involve precision-landings above hazard fields and slowing your momentum. It's not fun at all.

Review - Marble Mayhem: Fragile Ball

I'm always keen to try out a new marble madness-esque game.  Fragile Ball  is basic 2D 'marble' game of skill, with one simple goal of using gravity to get your ball to the exit, while avoiding the inevitable traps. Certainly sounds simple, but in practice its one hell of a challenge!  Hard is perhaps an understatement. Level design plays a big role in this, with plenty of hazards to avoid, placed in just the right spots to have you pulling out your hair. Some level design reminded me of the old classic, Crazy Machines, where one small incorrect move and it all falls apart in milliseconds, followed by a swift restart while you mumble to yourself that you can do better. There are also other levels though that are more open/scrolling, but regardless of the level type the restarts will be many! It can be brutal .. I found myself swearing & groaning at my screen on more than one occasion. I do enjoy a challenge though; something that takes practice.  With the high level of difficulty, I find this game is best suited to short sessions. 5-10mins over a coffee in the morning is good to wake the brain up. If I get stuck for too long, I stop to prevent the frustration building.   Along with more 'standard' levels previously mentioned, there are also some maze levels to challenge you. These are generally bigger levels allowing a larger degree rotation. Standard levels generally limit the range of angle you can choose giving more of a fixed direction - but this does vary quite a bit. Graphics are rather bland, along with animations and menus, but they do the job.  Although I do like the game overall, there are a few things that bugged me that I think could be improved upon. The mouse sensitivity has a limited range on the slider. With my Logitech mouse & slider all the way down, the movement still was too sensitive for my liking. This restricted the precision over the ball, but on reflection I can't be 100% sure if its just the mouse sensitivity or harsh physics in the game design.  Also found the maze levels when run in full screen made me feel nauseous. The spinning speed (and almost constant spinning sometimes), particularly when view full screen gave me some motion sickness. In a smaller screen (you can play in windowed mode) it was ok for me. Something to warn people about if they are sensitive to such things. Most levels were ok, but a few were tough to deal with.  Running in window mode was a bit problematic as well, as the mouse didn't lock to the game screen. I would move my mouse too far & it would flick back to windows, killing control over the ball.   I wouldn't recommend this to everyone (some will just find it infuriating!). It's not the best example I have seen in the genre with some flaws, but you are a gamer with patience & persistence, who likes a hardcore challenge then this is a good value puzzler to add to your collection. -Quick Review-   Marble Mayhem: Fragile Ball is a physics game developed by Bimboosoft Co.,Ltd. and released 2015.  Okay real talk, do you remember those old wooden maze games with the number holes, and the little steel ball you would navigate through the maze by tilting the maze up down, left or right? After a sequence of google searches I've come up with the title 'Labyrinth marble game'. Take that concept, and make a game out of it. BAM, that's Marble Mayhem Fragile Ball, and depending on your opinion of that retro physical game, that will effect your opinion on this game. Full disclaimer: I'm terrible at the real life version. Do read on!  http://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=757478124     -Detailed breakdown review-    Gameplay:  Easiest controls I can describe: Mouse to tilt right and left. BAM! Review done, roll the credits.  Okay, I can elaborate more on it. Some people seem to have problems with mouse sensitivity, I did notice you can tilt slightly with the keyboard but I pity you if you need to rely on the right and left arrows; I didn't try any levels with them. Pretty decent physics sandbox, requiring a very patieint and deliberate approach. With the angular level geometry, carefully positioned for ramps and stalls, it reminds me a lot of ElastoMania from the Windows 98 era.  There were 100 levels, and I got through about 50 of them in my two and a half hour play time. I see the levels as split into a few basic categories:  - Satisfying levels I was able to complete with enough persistence  - Tricky levels I restarted repeatedly but finally got through mostly on luck  - Impossible levels which I still don't even understand how to attempt  The visuals were fine, with some nicely responsive and helpful shadows reflecting your current angle of rotation. Several map themes (specifically the narrow brick pattern) made it difficult to discern ground from whitespace at first glance.  Controls may be overly sensitive, but to be fair I didn't fiddle with the singular control available in the Settings menu. Mouse movement felt digital rather than analog, with movements frequently reduced to discrete 'steps' rather than a fluid spectrum. But this wasn't entirely a downside, as it actually made it easier to re-attempt strategies on subsequent attempts.  Overall, I enjoyed my experience with this game, but would be pretty unlikely to come back to it. I got a good sampling of nearly all of the levels (some in row 2 refused to unlock even though I had completed all of their surrounding spaces) and respect the variety of showcases on display; the creator obviously had a deep understanding of their physics engine to create the optimal routes. I got this game in a bundle, for the price of $0.50, and it was easily worth that much and more; I've certainly thrown more money into arcade machines for much less of an experience. It goes on sale and is bundled often enough that you should be able to find it for less, but I would be comfortable to say it's worth its asking price.

Have you ever dreamed of rolling a frustratingly delicate ball around garbage maps made from the clearance section of your local Home Depot, all while listening to music that wouldn't be out of place in that weird Italian restaurant no one ever ate at but inconspicuously stayed open all through your childhood (You know the one, the parking lot was always empty save for that one car that never moved)? Well boy golly, have I got good news for you! Your dreams can come true today, yes all that I mentioned above, with the added bonus of the ball being so fragile you could swear it’s made from the purest of frozen orphan tears. Now I know, you're probably exhilarated, but contain your enthusiasm, because there's more. The engine has almost no concept of friction, so the slightest twitch sends that little ball flying through the air like a majestic, infuriating eagle, almost certain to detonate on impact when it lands a mere 15 inches away. The lack of friction is especially rewarding when the level has tiny, moving platforms, which require you to have the hand dexterity of a Himalayan Monk.  Seriously though, if you're into really difficult, repetitive puzzles/mazes/pachinko-with-the-added-threat-of-death type roll the ball games, this game can actually be pretty fun. Aesthetically, it looks like a demo for a game that's still in development, with textures and level design being reused so frequently the deja-vu gave me a concussion. The font is reminiscent of a Chuck E Cheese pizza menu only instead of a birthday party with that cool tube-gym with that awesome twisty slide you get pain and a chance to try out those cool curse words you’ve been waiting to use.  6/10, would suggest waiting until its on-sale

Challenging but unpolished puzzle game.  I played 15 of the 28 levels in under an hour. The game is based on rolling or tumbling shapes (ball, cube, brick, cylinder, ...) through a labyrinth. Where it gets tricky is when you need to color each square of ground, or have restrictions tumbling (low ceiling), or you have time restrictions (labyrinth being bombed, conveyor belt). Some of these levels are very good.  The problems is the time-limited levels that you need to redo at each failure, and because the author likes long introductions (the game starts with a voice mail from space), that means spending a lot of time on these attempts getting past the easy stuff to fail yet again at something that is only revealed when it is too late (maybe a wrong turn in the labyrinth or a problem coming up on the conveyor that is obscured by other parts of the level). On the other hand, the game never lets you get into a new mechanic you've learned by providing a few more levels like it; instead, it prefers to throw a different mechanic at you quickly. Add to that a general lack of polish (changing the resolution always sets it immediately, no way to set SFX and cheap BGM volume separately, mixed quality of art style, getting stuck tumbling down the stairs because the game is using a general physics engine for what is essentially constrained movement), and my feelings about this game are mixed.  If the timed puzzles were optional, and if there were more levels, or if the game was cheaper, I'd recommend it, because I really liked some of the challenges. But as it is, I expect many buyers are going to be disappointed.

Don't be fooled by the trailer. This game is completely vapid and devoid of any actual puzzles, at least for the first half an hour.  The game runs at 40fps; for such a simple game, this should not happen. More on this later.  The first shape you get introduced to is a sphere. Yawn, how boring. A ball-rolling 'puzzle' game. We have tons of those on Steam.  The second shape you get introduced to is a cube. Oh, how original; this CLEARLY didn't rip off EDGE.  Furthermore, the levels involving the cube are extremely buggy (you can often clip through walls or get stuck in mid-air), and the 40fps framerate makes the cube move too extremely slowly. Oh, did I mention that the first two cube levels are glass mazes? Because they are. Seriously, dev, mazes where you can't see the walls are even worse than FPS games.  Then there's the infamous Level 7; the cube starts off on a path which gets destroyed by a meteor, and cannot clear the path in time when the game is running at 40fps. Furthermore, while the cube seems to barely clear the path and is standing on solid ground, the 'falling off of path' sound plays and the level restarts! This bug has made it impossible for me to progress any further, and within this half an hour of a supposed 'puzzle game', I have not encountered a single puzzle that is not a maze.  Add to that the other misgivings in level design (i.e. punishing the player for not knowing something they couldn't have known before playing, or punishing the player for seeking a more efficient solution), UI and options (It's 2015 and you still don't have 1080p as a resolution?! There's no way to rebind keys or skip cutscenes?! Your game's UI is giant and obnoxious?!), and I can safely say that this game is one which I wish to refund. Unfortunately, I cannot do so since I bought this last winter, so that's £3.49 down the drain.  While it's no Journey Of The Light, even May's Mysteries: The Secret Of Dragonville is better than this, since that game actually started off with puzzles instead of time-wasting, buggy messes.  Developers, take note: If you can't show any puzzles in your 'puzzle' game within the first half an hour, why would the player continue playing? If your game's first half hour of gameplay is riddled with bugs, what reason do the players have to believe that the rest of it isn't? If your game's first half hour is not at all innovative or original, where is the 'innovative and original gameplay' that developers like you implicitly promise us?  All in all, developers, this game is exactly what a puzzle game should NOT look like.

First of all, this game seems to be extremely hardware demanding (built with cryengine and features lots of foliage, lighting, soft particles, etc). It was kind of unexpected from a game bundled with random pixel platformers. Anyway, if you have lags or input issues, lower the in-game resolution. I have a GT 640 and only managed to get stable 30 fps on 720p.  The gameplay itself is as frustrating as the game is demanding. I'm actually surprised I managed to beat the 6 levels it offers, having been ready to give up on several occasions.  The controls are... well, I can't call them completely 'unresponsive', but they sure feel stiff. Maybe they're supposed to be that way since you're controlling a giant globe after all, but there are lots of platforming sequences where you have to be quick and precise, and it's really hard to do because the controls complicate things. Especially until you get a 'double jump' and 'dash' abilities after beating levels 2 and 3.  The checkpoint placement is decidedly infuriating more often than not. At the end of the game I even had an impression that something glitched and the game simply stopped registering checkpoints mid-level.  Speaking of glitches, they happen occasionally and become more frequent the further you get. The aforementioned abilities (double jump, dash and float, although I didn't use the last one even once - it's literally not needed anywhere) interact with the environment in a weird way, sometimes making things cheat-like easy, sometimes being useless, sometimes working not as you expect them to, sometimes glitching out crazily.  The most outrageous thing in my opinion is the game's automated return system (a flying magical mask) that is supposed to return your ball to a checkpoint when it falls off the ledge. And it indeed does so, but not only when the ball falls, but apparently when it goes whenever it is 'not supposed' to go. Situations like  'Oh, look, the road splits! Oh, I can even go there!... What, back to the checkpoint? Why?!'  happen frequently, especially on laters levels. Sometimes you will be thrown back just for simply touching the edge of the way. Yeah, why bother making obstacles and invisible walls when we can just punish the player for being curious, right? And what's even funnier, sometimes the game suddenly decides to go non-linear on you, placing the collectible orbs off the beaten path or even offering two possible ways across the platforming area. So go figure when you're allowed to stray and when you're not.  To conclude, if you were attracted by pretty and relaxing panoramas on the store page's screenshots, don't be fooled - the game will keep you tense and irritated, the visuals being the only soothing thing about it. But if you got it in a bundle, well... you might as well give it a go.

Rolling Sun: ~~~~~~~~~   In the wold of Incas and Mayans, Gods were really influential in their civilization. One of them is the Sun God! You will now represent this god through the ball of magic stone in this stunning 3d environment.    Rolling Sun is a platformer/ adventure game where you are in control of the ball of magic stone. You will have to show your skill to manoeuvre this globe through obstacles in these well-designed levels. This is all about dexterity and timing. Let me elaborate a little bit about it. . . the physics of the ball are really well done and every small or subtle movement you make can determine really quickly whether you succeed a hurdle or have to start all over again. On each level you will have to get all the orb stones without falling down crevasses or touch water and you will….. Guess what!! Do it again!   You will be able to make your ball jump and this can led you to interesting situations, especially with these floating round platforms! These are very tricky to negotiate as they lean backward or forward if you do not land straight in the middle of them, which can influence whether or not you have to start all over again. Reach the end of a level and you will get a new ability.  I am extremely impressed with the presentation of this game - graphically it is stunning. From the control point of view, either you use the keyboard or the gamepad; they are sensitive and will take you a little bit of time to get use to them but they are fine. The soundtrack is very good, too, and fits the game very well.  Positive: ~~~~~~~   - Very well-designed levels - Stunning graphics - Very well priced  Negatives: ~~~~~~~~   - No achievements or trading cards - No indicators to find out how many orbs you have to collect  Rolling Sun is very well presented with stunning graphics. A different and enjoyable platformer/ adventure game. Worth having in your game library!  7.9/10  Key provided by developer/publisher for review purposes. Rolling Sun feels more like a half-finished thought than a complete game.  You're a rolling blue ball that can jump. You'll roll through some pretty envionments but that's really all there is to it. Challengers seem to be more co-incidental than by design. And are mostly the challenge is caused by the camera. The ball is centered in the screen even though every stage scrolls to the right. At speed you can jump significantly further than the amount of screen that can be seen. This is a problem because it reduces landing to luck. Or rolling very very slowly.  The physics sections are silly, I'm on the third of what looks like six stages (in less than half an hour) and nothing I've encounted so far has needed more thought than mashing the jump button. As long as a piece of stage mesh has been touched you can jump again so wall climbing is doable. With that said the physics on the floating rafts is annyoing because they bob up and down quite fast; and impart interia when jumped off making it impossible to judge far you'll jump.  There are switches in the game. There should not have been switches in the game. Rolling into a swtich triggers a long switch rotation animation which is bad. Worse is that whatever is switched doesn't start animating until after the switch animation is over. This makes it easy to trigger a swtich, wait, roll out of the switch and then roll down a hole because the platforms raised by the switch are still raising. What was the point? Everyting switchable could have been left permanently in place without the aggravation of having to switch it  There is no gameplay challenge. There is no fail condition. You can fall down holes as often as you like, you'll be placed back at the start of the jump afterwards. There are blue balls to collect but no indication of how many you need to collect - if any at all. There is no timer so there is no time pressure. Roll slowly and you should have no problem at all.  Lastly I've run into a few glitches in the short time I've played. Big red textures saying replace me, getting stuck behind the far side of the level. And still having ball control whilst being rescued from a hole. When given the strafe power-up the jump button re-binds from A to Y and strafe left becomes A; which is confusing.  All-in-all Rolling Sun is not a game I'd recommend unless you're looking for something very laid back.

Your ball has a ridiculous amount of inertia, meaning that most of your time is spent hitting obstacles and standing still -- even worse if you're trying to proceed upslope. It gives you just enough side-to-side pseudo-3D 'freedom' to screw you up by running you into ground roughness that throws you off your path and sends you into pits, and if you try to take advantage of that to find better routes, you run into invisible walls. I am not an unskilled gamer (I've made it through most of I Wanna Be The Guy) and I still found myself stuck for upwards of three minutes after falling into the first pit in the first level. The provided step isn't high enough for your jump to get you out, and trying to build momentum by running in circles in the pit slams you either into invisible walls or the step, both of which stop you dead, so you have to basically wade around in molasses until you manage to bounce off the step at just the right angle to hop back into play.   That, and fighting with the game to gett its screen resolution right on my dual-monitor setup, was my entire 15-minute play experience. Game deleted with prejudice.

Rolling Sun is a pretty game.  A pretty bad one.  This game might as well be an advertisement for the Cryengine’s resources; this game makes use of the Cryengine’s built-in resources to build a very pretty game. There’s beautiful landscapes, nice vistas, breathtaking rivers…  And very little fun to be had, sadly.  The game itself is a basic platformer. You control a spherical rock (possibly one of the stone spheres of Costa Rica, though it has ornate, glowing designs over the surface), and this matters – your rock will roll off of inclined slopes and has a fair bit of weight to it, which can tax some of the floating platforms. You start off having only the ability to roll around and jump, but over the course of the game you acquire the ability to double jump, air dash, and float (a much slower rate of descent) at the end of the second, third, and fourth levels respectively. While this sounds like it would add more gameplay, it honestly doesn’t; double jumping is the only ability that actually ends up important, and while you can use the other abilities, they’re never really necessary.  The game consists of six fairly short levels with checkpoints distributed throughout them. The checkpoints are invisible but are mostly fairly generous, with the exception of the end of the final level, where it feels like half the level feeds off of one checkpoint. Not that it really matters in terms of difficulty; there’s only a few sections (such as one bit where there’s a moving platform underneath you that moves forward, reassembling itself before you – with or without you, if you’re too slow) that are really challenging platforming.  Instead, the game has the lovely aspect of being “3D”, but being more like those old beat-’em-up games where you can move across a narrow space, but are mostly just moving left to right. However, if you move outside of these bounds, sometimes you’ll run into an invisible wall (okay), and sometimes you’ll get picked up by a floating Mayan mask which drags you back to the last checkpoint as if you fell off the level. This discourages you from poking around and exploring… not that there’s anything to explore, really.  It takes until the third level of the game for it to do anything different, at which point it starts having sections that lead away from the camera into the distance (and, at a few painful points, head towards the camera, which thanks to the narrow field of view makes it hard to see where you’re going).  Each level is filled with collectables – namely, a small floating rock with a blue field around it. They’re basically the game’s equivalent of coins, and they’re all over the place and mostly are used to show the proper way forward. If you collect every one of them in every level, you’ll unlock four bonus stages, which are shorter than the main levels and contain no checkpoints and the most challenging platforming in the game (though they’re still not all that hard).  The further the game goes on, the weaker it gets; the first few levels feel fairly organic, but by the end of the game it often feels fairly arbitrary in terms of the level design, and the graphical quality also declines in the second half of the game, with pop-in issues rearing their head in the fourth level, followed by a rather drab nighttime level and a final snow level which is very generic and doesn’t even let your ball make paths in the snow in its wake.  All in all, the game is just not worth it. It is about an hour and a half long if you want to get and play all the content, but there’s really just not much here; very basic platforming with mediocre at best level design consisting of platforms, bridges, and similar things over bottomless pits. There aren’t any enemies to speak of, no story… it is just a rather empty experience.  Pretty, but pretty pointless to play.

A lot of reviews complained about this game, especially the performance, but when I saw that it was 49 cents I decided to give it a shot.   Performance: On my older mainstream enthusaist computer (i5-750, 760 GTX), I was getting good framerates on High graphics @ 1080p. I'd guess about 45-52 FPS. No screen tearing at all. At the beginning of stage 3 there is a really choppy part - there's some kind of optimization error there and I had to reduce it to Low graphics @ 800x600 -- luckily, no restart is required for any graphics changes so I just made it past that part and put the graphics back up.   The game is a little short -- I beat it my first time playing, in about 1.5 hours. I died quite a few times but you start back at a checkpoint. There are some extras and bonus levels you can unlock.   There doesn't seem to be any statisics tracking or goals. The game should have allowed you to try to beat your time and other things but there's nothing to it but to make it through the level. Also, it seems like the ball could have had a higher top speed especially downhill. They never explain why you are collecting the orbs but you'll notice that you need to collect all the orbs to unlock some bonus levels.   The game doesn't have the polish of a Nintendo game or anything but it's also not $50.00. The graphics are very good especially on the last stage; the sound is just the basics; the music is okay but there are only 2 songs which alternate and get tiresome; the control is pretty good but they could have taken it a step further and changed the handling based on the surface like sand or ice; the physics are pretty good; the level design is pretty good; the ability to gain powers is pretty cool but mostly only the double jump gets used.   It just seems like the developers got bored of working on this instead of spending the time it would take to make the game special and hold your interest. Pretty much the entire time I played I wished that they would have used this game world for an RPG or hack and slash platform game instead.  I own thousands of games and don't normally play games for this long so I guess I enjoyed the challenge and appreciated that I didn't have to start over from the beginning when I died which allowing me to enjoy the entire game. I recommend it on sale if you have a decent computer and don't mind switching the graphics low in the first part of stage 3.

TLDR: This game is right at the threshold between a Thumbs Up and Thumbs Down review. The early levels of the game are painful, but the final levels are quite fun.   You roll around with a ball and must interact with the environment to progress. You use your own weight to activate switches, raise and lower platforms, etc. As a platformer, it is pretty basic, but it does well with what it can offer in terms of game play mechanics.  Controls are difficult. The ball is sluggish to respond to your inputs, occasionally not responding at all, and it seems physically impossible to roll in a straight line. Anytime you jump, your ball seems to propel itself forward, almost always overshooting the platform you were aiming for.  You unlock new abilities as you progress through the game: a double jump, dash forward and backwards, and a floating ability that slows the balls descent rate. These abilities are never actually utilized by the level design, so it results in an inverted difficulty curve. The early levels of the game are brutally difficult, but the later levels are much easier because you have a bunch of abilities to save yourself when you fall of the course. I wonder if the sole purpose of the abilities are to offset the terrible controls.  The environment is gorgeous, but there are too many foreground elements that constantly block your view. The depth of field is also so narrow that you can't see what is coming immediately in front of you, often causing you to roll into a pit. I sometimes found that I couldn't even tell where I was supposed to roll in order to continue the level. Two of the ten levels in the game provide a view into the screen that shows what is coming in front of you. I think the game would have been significantly more enjoyable if more levels used this perspective.  This all combines for a game with a cool idea but poor execution. You'll go through a lot of trial and error gameplay that is far more frustrating than it is worth in the early levels. However, the final few levels of the game are incredibly fun, particularly the final bonus level, and I'd say the game is worth playing for those levels alone.

This isn't really a platformer (you don't have much control over the bombs) but it's more like The Incredible Machine or Lemmings. The bombs enter the level from a set point and you have a handful of tools you can use to send the bombs where you want them to go. Gravity is enough to get them started but when they stall out, they roll into each other and explode, which means the bomb in front gets a boost from the bomb behind it. This can create some very interesting and surprising situations, especially on levels where you have more tools available. (What tools you have varies from level to level.)  Ultimately the goal is to blow up all the rocks on the level that have gems in them so you can collect money from them and move onto the next level. As you beat levels you get experience points that help you unlock other kinds of bombs that have special abilities, as well as upgrades for bombs you already have.  Because it's a puzzle game, there are levels when you're probably going to get stuck. There are hints available for every level you can activate if you're at that point where it's going from fun to frustrating, but I haven't had that happen. (Yet.)  +Pros: Lots of levels with lots of possible solutions. A pretty concise tutorial and good controls.   -Cons: You cannot move tools around while bombs are moving. I understand why they did this but there are moments when it can slow down the pace of the game till you learn how it works.

After 2.3 hours I decided to write a review.  TLDR - If you like Lemmings you will like this.   Pros- Fluid gameplay. The bombs consistently react the same which was my big concern for gameplay. Aesthetically the game is nice to look at and has a sort of vintage feel. Original music. Surprisingly clever challenges later on.   Cons- There is only 2 speeds to play the game at (normal and slightly fast forwarded) which slowed me down when I tried a shotgun/try every combination approach to a puzzle I couldn't solve.   All in all this game is a fun and solid experience that is both relaxing and a bit of a brain teaser. There are some small quirks (like bombs burning the foilage) that I thought were a nice touch. I hadn't played a puzzle platform game like this in years and so this was a nice surprise in that it had a sort of old timey feel to it. For the price there seems to be a surprising amount of gameplay there, especially compared to the last few indie games I've bought, so I would definitely put this on my recommended list.

To go into a little more detail, character creation begins with race and class selections, there are 4 playable races to choose, dwarf, human, elf, and demon. Currently only humans and demons are selectable. I am not sure if elves and dwarves are locked because they are unfinished and unimplemented yet, or if they are some sort of bonus you get for something. Class wise there are 9 that I remember, the classes are gender locked. The 9 classes are Barbarian, paladin, warrior, ranger, monk, assassin, sorcerer, priest and necromancer.  Currently I am leveling an Assassin, so far throughout the demon starting zone my experience has been solid, dated, but definitely decent. Overall I feel that Sphere 3: enchanted world does not do very much different from MMO's that were out 5- 10 years ago. It does however manage to keep what made many of those MMOs decent. I would recommend it to anyone who is a fan of classic MMO's

--OVERVIEW-- I just got this game on release day, and I must, say, it's surprising! Puzzle Ball is, in essence, a spiritual successor to marble-based games like Marble Blast Gold, Ballance and Marble Madness. Being a lover of Marble Blast Gold, I thought that this couldn't hurt and gave it a try. After playing with a few of the scenario levels and checking out the level editor, I must say that this game is amazingly fun for 3 dollars. This game is not as much of a skill platformer as others in its genre, but is more of a puzzle, like the name implies. Figuring out the order in which to accomplish challenges for a high score is important, as some points can be permanently missed if you don't do them at the right times. However, there is never so much chalenge that you will get angry at the game, as the game does live up to its 'casual' tag This, the beautiful graphics, and the relaxing music combine to create a surprisingly fun experience, as watching each levels' mechanisms come to life is fascinating, and there is some satisfaction in completing each level.  --THE EDITOR-- In addition, the level editor is quite easy to use, as the description states. It is a simple 'pick block and place' style editor. However, the camera and controls of the editor are a bit weird, so there is definitely room for improvement there. Other than that, there isn't too much for me to say about the level editor, as I'm not into taht sort of thing.  >NOTE: There is a 'level budget,' so you cannot make infinitely big levels! :(  --MENUS-- This is where my criticisms start. After launching the game, you will be treated to a small graphic informing you of the controls. There seems to be no way to bring this up again besides restarting the game. After dealing with the graphic, you will be treated to a menu with no logo and four buttons: 'Levels,' 'Editor,' 'Options' and 'Quit.' Clicking 'Levels' takes you to a bland screen with the 11 scenario leves shown, with the options to look at user levels. Clicking 'Editor' throws you straight into the editor with no options or preparation screen. Selecting 'Options' brings you to an options screen where you can edit your screen resolution, quality (idk what this exactly means), your languages (choices of English, Russian, and Dutch), something called 'Image Resolution' (I really have no idea what this does), your sound/music volumes, whether to be fullscreen/windowed, bloom, and SSAO. There is no way to rebind key controls, although they are standard (WASD) and you shouldn't have trouble with them. While the menus certainly are functional, they are bland and lack depth; but as this is a 3 dollar game, it is acceptable.  --PROS-- >Interesting gameplay >Very nice graphics >Relaxing music >Infinite replayability with the level editor >Good learning curve  --CONS-- >Only 11 built-in levels >Lame menus >Some typical functionality missing (rebinding controls, advanced graphics, etc.) >Small music selection  --VERDICT--  >9/10< Despite a few flaws, this game is simply astounding for 3 dollars. I don't know how many people these days have played or even heard of Ballance, and I have no idea how many other games are similar to Ballance or what Ballance got its ideas from, but Puzzle Ball feels like a worse made version of some of those other marble puzzle games.  Either way Ballance is rather old, and doesn't have a level editor. The puzzles in Puzzle Ball are pretty fun though extremely easy, but with the level editor the possibilities are endless but since I'm not a creative type I doubt I'll see much use out of it.  What makes the game bad? The music is terrible, a mouse cursor always flashes in the middle of the screen, the menus overlap, there's no 'next level' option when you beat a level, you can't actually close menus in 2-player mode without exiting the stage or restarting the level, deaths are rather meaningless since there's no lives or penalty that I can see, and only about half of the vital text is in English, the other half in Dutch or something. This made the tutorial totally useless, but the idea is pretty easy: use WASD or the arrow keys to guide your ball to the end using two other ball types (a stone and a paper mache ball) to solve the various puzzles. Each ball is better at different things, like paper being able to go over water (but wood can't float enough apparently) and stone being able to do some heavy hitting and fall through glass.  Other irks are the vertical split screen, horizontal would do better on some monitors and having the wider angle is easier to see anyway. It takes too long to load a level, I don't know why it has to do each individual block over the course of 10 seconds (and this on a not-weak-by-any-definition computer). The level editor has a block limit (come on we're on the PC here) and I wish a few of the graphics blended in a tad better. There aren't nearly enough actual levels (or scenarios) which I'm guessing is the purpose of the user-made levels, which, as you expect, range from absolutely terrible to waste of time impossibly hard. I also seemed to unlock achievements while idling on the home screen, and I'd get the same achievement 13 times after that. Weird.  What's good about it? The controls are good, the graphics are good, the puzzles are good, and this game is cheap as Puzzle Balls. Value wise this is a great buy, but game wise it still needs work and feels unfinished, or at least 'we worked hard on this game, it's close enough, let's release it without smoothing out the rest' finished. So far best Steam Wallet buy but least favorite marble puzzle game buy.

Hyper Bounce Blast  is the latest game from Flump Studios, which you may have heard of from their successful titles, such as Horizon Shift.  Always faithful to the genre,  Hyper Bounce Blast  is a sweet and delicious homage to the 80-90's Shm'up wave, and it succeeds wonderfully in offering unique gameplay mechanics.  You're controlling a bouncing ship with the ability to wall jump and bounce on the ennemies.  As long as you're in the air, you're entirely invincible from every form of threat. But if you land on the ground, you'll be vunerable ! As compensation, you will also get to collect the points from the kills you've just made. And if you reach the ceiling, you will bank your chain.  And that is what the game is mostly about. You need to focus either on jumping or shooting, or maybe both if you're awesome like that.  Oh, should I talk about the Hyper ? When your Hyper bar is full, you can release your full power, and give headaches to your ennemies by going BWAAAAAAAAAAAAH for a few seconds. This can save your life, really. And give you hell of a lot of points, secondarily, but make sure to activate it as close as you can from the top of the screen!  As usual, you have access to different game modes, each with their own leaderboards. While I do wish the game the success it deserves, I must admit I love the small community it currently gathers, just for the fact you can have a say with your scores, as modest as they are. It's way more rewarding than ending up in the 100th page of leaderboards, where nobody will ever find you again.   I found  Hyper Bounce Blast  graphically stunning, and it runs smoother than ever. Every new game from the Studios is yet another big step towards indie professionalism (careful not to go too far, or you'll get tired, Paul!), and I'm really excited to see what is next to come out of their magic hat of high-quality games.  Whether you're a retro gamer, shmup-lover, or simply someone who wants to discover that genre, I can only recommend  Hyper Bounce Blast  : it is made with passion, doubtlessly.

Target Audience:     SHMUP fans wanting an alternative experience.      Summary:   If you're looking for the same old same old from the SHMUP experience, you can look away from Hyper Bounce Blast. Just like Horizon Shift, it makes a small twist in the genre by adding a platforming mechanic, and that mechanic is well implemented in terms of gameplay. There's something satisfying to bouncing from enemy to enemy while shooting everything in site. And this core gameplay feels fresh in the genre, even if it may not have a lot of staying power over the long haul. Look, this is a 5 dollar game, and there are things that could have raised the game to the next level in terms of replayability, such as some random enemy formats or different options. But the core experience keeps thing simple and yet fun, allowing you to focus on small simple bite-sized elements in the game that combine to a good couple hour experience. It's a developer that doesn't want to make the same old game: he's experimental: and not in the “artsy” type of way. It's the gameplay mechanics he plays with: and I will openly admit, I'm always fascinated by those who try something different in a genre that usually keeps things safe. And good on Flump studios for producing games that change things up: and deliver an enjoyable experience.   Video Review:           YouTube™ Video:  Hyper Bounce Blast (5 Minute Review)

Arcade Arrange  Start with zero lives and work your way through all the phases of the game. Disclaimer - Developer submitted me a free key for the game for review purposes.   Hyper Bounce blast is an interesting take on the Shmup genre. By combining it with elements of platform games and puzzle games, Hyper Bounce Blast is a unique, if unimpressive shooter.  The idea is to shoot the red enemies, and jump on the blue enemies while collecting fragments that the red ships leave behind. Once you've gained a plethora of these fragments, the aim is to 'bank' the points by jumping to the top of the screen before the wave ends.  The vector styled graphics suit the game well, and controller support is tight and responsive. It also makes you brain think asymmetrically as you have to figure out which enemies to shoot and when to shoot them, as shooting a blue enemy renders it unable to be jumped on, and jumping on enemies is the only way to make your ship impervious to enemy fire.   While the ideas around the game are great, keyboard and mouse movement lacks finesse, and it's very easy to lose track of your subtly coloured aiming reticle. The bosses and bullet patterns are also unfortunately very generic, seemingly ripped directly from Cave Shmups.  That being said, the game has a definitely high difficulty curve, and the price is right, so if you fancy a challenge, it's worth taking a look at. It's a good game, but not a great one. Disclosure: I was given a free key by the developer.  -=The Good=-  Stylish vector visuals Good music Interesting combination of gameplay styles Solid controls Centipede-inspired bonus levels Multiple game modes   -=The Bad=-  Unkillable enemies Occasional cheap deaths Low powerup drop rate Slow 'Hyper' filling   -=The Details=-  The game itself is an interesting combo-pack of ideas, some of which are borrowed from Flump Studios' previous game, Horizon Shift (HS). From the vector graphic-designed enemies that look like they could have been in HS, to the animation playing faintly behind all of the action, it screams HS in look and presentation. However, the similarities end there for the most part. This is basically a twin-stick shooter, as you control the gun with the right stick, and movement with the left. But rather than just move around freely over the entire play area ala Smash TV or Robotron 2084, you're main area is along the bottom of the screen not unlike Space Invaders or Galaga. From there, you'll go after the red and green enemies for score and bonuses while avoiding their bullets by either moving/jumping out of the way, or bouncing off of blue objects to make yourself invincible.  Yes, you heard right, you'll be jumping and bouncing in this game. By jumping onto a low-moving blue object (or using a wall jump like in NES' Ninja Gaiden to reach a higher blue object), you become invincible to bullets and enemies. Not only that, the destroyed blue objects leave gems behind for you to collect either by hitting the floor and catching as many as you can as they fall, or by hitting the ceiling and getting them all. Another perk of the blue enemies is that bouncing off of them allows you to absorb bullets to fill up a Hyper meter that can be used to unleash a large blast that destroys most enemies (or get a big bonus... if you know how). As a bonus, if you can destroy groups of green ships, you gain a star. And if you collect five stars, you get taken to a bonus level at the end of the current stage to fight in what is clearly an homage to Centipede.  The action starts slow, but gradually builds into a frenzied skirmish of shooting, avoiding and collecting. The bosses in the game are the same way; starting off simple, but getting more demanding with each new one in terms of how you damage it and its bullet patterns. Thankfully, the controls are responsive and the hit detection seems to be on point as well. And as you frantically do all of this, you'll have some enjoyable music to listen to thanks to the OST that features catchy, synthy beats.  Sounds good, right? And for the most part, it is. But there are some issues with the game. First and foremost, are the unkillable enemies. This is a personal taste thing, but I HATE enemies you can't kill, especially when there are a lot of them. I've always felt they were a somewhat cheap way to add difficulty to a stage or section (I'm all for making a given enemy-type tough, but not indestructible). And sadly, this game features these undying things in the form of laser cannons that fire when you touch the ground, laser cannons that fire at timed intervals, and buzzsaws that go around the edges of the entire play area. All you can do is avoid them, which gets tedious after awhile and frustrating toward the end of the game... especially when they cause an unfair death.  Yes, this game has them too. There have been times where I beat the level, but triggered the floor laser cannons just as the level was ending. The result was the cannon's firing while the rest of the stage was blowing up. More than once, I found myself unavoidably falling into the laser blast and losing a life as the stage ended. I also encountered similarly unfair deaths after dropping from the ceiling. See, when you touch the ceiling and get all of the gems on-screen, you drop to the floor again. The problem is, you can't land on any blue objects as you fall. You just pass through them due to the invincibility you're given at that moment. When you hit the floor again, you become vulnerable again right away and that's where I got killed by bullet groups that I couldn't avoid thanks to how hectic things start getting around the mid-way point of the game.  A final pair of complaints come from the way powerups are handed out and how long it takes to fill the Hyper meter. It seems as if the powerups drop rather infrequently, and I've yet to figure out if it's because I'm not doing something right/often enough to trigger them, or if the game's just stingy with them. Either way, you really start feeling under-powered when you play through 15 stages and only get one powerup (if you're lucky). Lastly, the Hyper meter always seems to take forever to fill. And as if that weren't enough, I've watched it get emptied out without using it or dying. I'm still trying to figure out if that last part's intentional, or a bug in the game.  So in the end, what can be said about Hyper Bounce Blast? It's a fun little game and at 30 somewhat short levels, it can be a one-sitting type of game as well. The visuals, the music, the gameplay, several modes to choose from... it all works together pretty well to make for an entertaining game that keeps you on your toes. But issues like questionable deaths, unkillable enemies and some potentially iffy powerup frequency choices put a few blemishes on this game's vector graphics-inspired visage. So while it is a game I recommend, it's one that could have used a few tweaks in my opinion.  Score- 7.5 / 10
