When you first boot up Marble Mountain, you probably won't be impressed. The graphics look very cheap, the music sounds like some sort of cheap royalty-free track, and the noises made by the 'skull' enemies that soon appear are just awful. It doesn't help that later in the game, the larger levels are very poorly marked and you will spend a decent amount of time trying to figure out which direction you're meant to go, and there's one particular desert-themed level that is just complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.  But you know what? I really like this game, for three main reasons:  1. Maybe it's just me, but I can't find a good old-fashined marble run game on Steam. Maybe they went out of fashion, but I really like the balancing act of manuevering many imaginative obstacles and occasional light puzzles and maintaining control over my marble.  2. The controls are sublime. It's really easy to control your marble without losing too much control, yet when you have to maneuver across a sloped surface, you can almost FEEL the marble trying to roll away. it's smooth, it's responsive, and I love it.  3. Despite the poor layout, I'm genuinely impressed by the design of the levels. The developer has clearly put some thought into building the world that you navigate, and there is a great amount of variety to the obstacles and puzzles. The levels are never just plain single-coloured blocks with the occasional decoration but fully fleshed out scenes and structures, and it genuinely feels like your little marble is going on an adventure.  In addition to the above, at the time of writing, I'm up to a level simply titled 'Tricksy', and that is when ♥♥♥♥ gets real and the developer kicks his design ideas up a notch.  VR support is also a bonus. Admittedly, I can't review this as I don't have VR equipment at home, but I imagine it's quite cool. Having support for both Steam and third-party VR is a great idea from the developer, too.  TL;DR: Buy it when it's on sale.  Pros: - clever level design - great controls - good old-fashioned fun - VR support  Cons: - looks cheaply made - poor level layout - that one ♥♥♥♥ing desert level - annoying music & SFX

This game... where to begin.  Let's start with the good points, I guess.  Pro: The ball rolls about as you would expect, I guess? The game actually runs very well for a UE4 title, probably because of its simplicity. Some of the level designs are interesting if you can endure the rather uninteresting and tedious early levels.  Con: $4 pricetag for essentially an asset swap in what seems more like a hobbyist project than a commercially viable game. $1, perhaps, $4, no thanks.  Blatant asset flip. You will be watching a generic blue/lightblue ball roll across the two generic sci-fi hex patterns that are featured in UE4 for the majority of the time. Most of the other assets remind me of generic space assets, probably freely available. While this isn't necessarily a bad thing, again, there is $4 pricetag. Considering that the achievement art looks like it was tossed together in paint and the menus are reminiscent of 2003, I'd say that this is not a particularly artistically endowed game. Again, you don't have to be a great artist, but a commercial game project typically doesn't just recycle art. The music is also generic and loopy. Physics get wonky when two or more things colide at once, and surfaces behave unnaturally. The friction of the ball on the generic platform does not correspond to how it looks like it should.  Early levels are tedious and uninteresting. The camera is kind of uncomfortable to adjust, and the menu does not lock the camera.  While this game shows some okay principles underlying the gameplay, the actual design of the game is less satisfying and definitely does not justify the pricetag, especially since it seems more like a 'hey, look at what I can do with Unreal Engine 4' than a finished product.

I forced myself to play through this entire game, expecting some challenging puzzles, but there are few to be had. The developer’s lack of any replies on the forum just adds to the sense that this was a half attempt at a game that he himself did not think it was worthy of his time to bother playing it through before selling it. Pros:  -Skip level feature. -Working achievements. -Handful of levels are nicely designed with a puzzle to solve. Cons: -Changing the quality setting in the game actually changes the way the ball moves. That’s right - some levels are easier or near impossible based on the set video quality. -Next button at the end of the stage sometimes skips ahead to some random level. I guess that could be a pro for speed-running it. -Using Continue from the main menu takes longer to load the level than selecting it from the level select menu. -The pause menu doesn’t actually pause the game, it just stops the ball’s movement, but then gravity still has an effect and brings it down.  -Closing the pause menu has to be done with the mouse and it moves the camera while doing so. -The camera defaults to a view where the ball is not in full view and you have to readjust the camera every time. -False advertising – the store page claims there are 8 unlockable skins, but these are nowhere to be seen in the game, even after completing all of the levels. -Broken levels. One level in particular, 31, has a rotating staircase that does not allow the player to ever make it to the top. I wasted at least an hour of my time before realizing that it just wasn’t going to happen.  I really wanted to enjoy this game, but not possible in its current state.

'Roll'd' is a really surprisingly fun game. I bought it due to my prefererence for SAS (short attention span) games and multiple levels to be unlocked with a gradual progression. Figured if I played for an hour it would be reasonable at this remarkably low price. After three days I have most of the achievements and have passed level 40 (of 50 for which achievements are offered.)  The premise of Roll'd is that instead of the character moving, the path does. Perhaps a small change, but a very nice variation from the norm. At various points new levels and variations are unlocked, as well as new and bizarre 'runners'. The numerous paths may only be different in appearance, but they certainly look VERY different, and give the feel of not being at all similar in gameplay. If it's an illusion, it's a good one.  The art and music of Roll'd are really nice, and all in all this is a remarkable game for this low price of less than a dollar. If you like dexterity or running games, Roll'd is certainly one to be considered near the top of the list for players of all ages.  Thank you.

Right off the bat, I wasn't sure what you think of the music. It's nice, yet at the same time, it got annoying after a while. I think the problem was mainly that it was the same music playing over, and over, and over again. I finally ended up just turning off the music. There are multiple characters to choose from, but this is done via an unlock/leveling up system. Map selection also goes off this as well. It's really nice they offer it as a leveling perk instead of just 'You beat the course, here's an unlock!' What's even better is that even if you die, you still get some levels depending on how far you got. Considering I'm terrible at this game, that was quite helpful for me.  The concept of Roll'd is pretty basic and fun. Don't roll and you win. Sounds easy, but it can be challenging, which is nice. I really enjoyed this game, even if I kept dying. One issue was that even if you were full screen, the actual game was not. It's weird because every other aspect about the game is full screen except for the actual gameplay. I suppose it's not as big of a deal, and doesn't make too big of a difference, but it'd still be nice if we're in full screen to actually have full screen gameplay.  There are actually quite a lot of high points about this game. Controller support, Steam achievements, trading cards, mlocal co-op, multiplayer, and even cross platform multiplayer. The developers really went all out on this game and made it very much Steam friendly. On top of this Roll'd is only 0.99 cents. Pretty good price for this. I took a look at the developer interaction, and from what I'm seeing, the last developer to community interaction was two weeks ago, and that was simply to step in for a forum moderation role. According to their Steam page, the last actual update was a month ago. Given how little the developer is interacting now, it worries me that they've given up on this game. If that is the case, it's a real shame, because Roll'd is very fun, and had a lot of possibilities.     Positives:       Character variety.    Unlock system. (you unlock from completing or failing a course)    Map variety.    Fun concept.    Controller support.    Steam achievements.    Trading cards.    Co-Op.    Multiplayer.    Cheap.     Negatives:       Even in full screen the game itself is not full screen.    Music gets annoying after a while.    No updates in over a month, and communication from the developers has ceased. This is a simple and enjoyable game with a few little niggles, but overall I had a pleasant experience. This is an endless runner game where you control the road the character is running on rather than the runner itself, which is an interesting idea. The music in the menus (there is no music when actually playing, presumably to aid with concentration) is poppy and fun and quite catchy.  There are multiple difficulty settings for each stage of the game, each of which needs to be unlocked by increasing your character level with each time you play awarding you XP based on your performance. Each difficulty setting requires you to be a certain level to unlock, and you have to unlock each difficulty setting in a stage to unlock the next one.  This is where I had an issue; with each stage unlocking in a linear fashion based on your level, you often spend a long time on the same stage to build your XP, just replaying it over and over again on the higher difficulty settings you unlock just to open up the next stage, which can get a little tedious. Personally, I would have liked to have seen several stages open up at once to give you more options so as to not have it feel so grindy, whilst getting a certain score perhaps in one difficulty setting could unlock the next one. Then have another block of stages open up at a certain character level.  But those niggles aside, I'd recommend this for people who like to play for just a few minutes at a time or even those masochists who enjoy an XP grind. I think you'll find a lot to like here.

This is a game that really makes me question the binary nature of reviews on Steam. This probably not a game I would recommend but that doesn't make it bad and I don't feel it deserves a thumbs down.  This is a game that you will probably only enjoy if you like Breakout clones. I haven't played much but the basic mechanics are straight forward: move a paddle back and forth bouncing a ball at bricks. What differentiates this from other Breakout clones is the fact that the ball has a small amount of gravity applied to it. Normally in Breakout the ball would just be an aimless floating object that went in one direction until it hit an obstacle. In Ball of Wonder we get something a little different; we get curvature. If you knock a ball too far to one side of the field, it will not bounce indefinitely until reaching the blocks as would normally happen in Breakout and is usually quite annoying to wait for. No, instead the ball will lose upward momentum and return to you in a reasonably timely fashion. This may not sound like much but in my opinion it's quite a big improvement over the normal mechanics. I only wish I could increase the gravity value just a tad, as the ball is still very floaty.  I don't see myself playing a lot of this, but I support the creator's outside-the-box thinking and would love to see what they might produce in the future.
